extracted.intended_audience: literary scholars, students, and researchers applying Barthes' narrative theory to short fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Roland Barthes' five narrative codes to interpret meaning and structure in a short story (here: Flannery O'Connor's 'Revelation'), locating codes in title, characters, objects, actions, images, and dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hermeneutic Code (Enigma Code)
rubrics_metrics.description: Denotes enigma or mystery in the narrative; creates curiosity and questions that propel interpretation (e.g., who received the revelation, why it occurred, what its purpose is).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify textual elements that generate unanswered questions or suspense: the title as enigma, ambiguous character motivations (Mrs. Turpin's contradictory religiosity and pride), waiting-room interactions that provoke curiosity. Use these enigmas to trace what the text withholds and how answers (or lack thereof) drive reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proairetic Code (Action Code)
rubrics_metrics.description: Composed of actions or events that move the story forward; sequential acts that create plot progression and suspense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locate concrete actions that trigger subsequent events (e.g., Mrs. Turpin's arrival and behaviour in the waiting room; Mary Grace's throwing of a book). Treat these acts as puzzle pieces whose ordering and causal links produce narrative momentum and climax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semantic Code (Connotative Code)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words, phrases, images, and details that carry additional connotative meanings beyond the literal, producing overtones and thematic resonance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to loaded words and descriptors ('ugly', 'Jesus', racial epithets, labels like 'white trash', 'well-dressed'), place-names and settings ('waiting room'), and objects (title of Mary Grace's book 'Human Development') to reveal social attitudes, value judgments, classism, and layered meanings. The semantic code often overlaps with binary oppositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic Code
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects, actions, images, and arrangements that have concealed or allegorical significance (symbols whose meanings operate across the text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify recurring images and their broader symbolic implications: the story's title echoing Biblical Revelation (judgment/eschatology), eyesight as 'window to the soul' and moral vision, pigs as emblematic of materialism/uncleanliness and purgatorial cleansing, and Mrs. Turpin's backyard vision of ascending souls. Use symbols to interpret spiritual and moral dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural Code (Referential Code)
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements that presuppose cultural, social, religious, or historical knowledge which contextualize the narrative (e.g., Christian beliefs, Southern US social norms, race and class structures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read characters' backgrounds, behaviours, and social markers against cultural frameworks: Christian iconography and doctrines, mid-twentieth-century southern US life, racial and class hierarchies. These referential elements explain motivations, social status, and interpretive possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binary Oppositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Contradictory pairs or oppositions in the text (e.g., good vs. evil, pride vs. acceptance, beauty vs. ugliness, white vs. black, wealth vs. poverty) that structure meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map the oppositions exhibited by characters, dialogue, and imagery (noting Mrs. Turpin vs. Mary Grace as paradigmatic). Use these binaries to highlight thematic tensions and social commentary; examine how the text affirms, subverts, or complicates such oppositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readerly vs. Writerly Text Distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification of texts as 'readerly' (closed, leading the reader to a predetermined end) or 'writerly' (open, inviting the reader to produce meanings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the narrative's structure and use of codes encourages passive reception (readerly/closed) or active interpretation (writerly/open). This classification affects how authorial control and readerly agency are weighed in analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locating Codes in Specific Textual Sites
rubrics_metrics.description: The five codes manifest in particular textual loci: title, characters, objects, actions, images, and dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematically search these sites for evidence of hermeneutic, proairetic, semantic, symbolic, and cultural codes — e.g., the title as hermeneutic/symbolic, characters' behaviour as proairetic/semantic, objects like books or pigs as semantic/symbolic. Use this methodological instruction to structure close-reading.
